Draw a diagram that represents the vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y)= -2xy \, \mathbf{i} + x^2 \, \mathbf{j}
$$

 at the points $(-2,1), (-1,-2),$ and $(1,-1).$
e-9440.worked_solution:
To sketch the vector field at the given points, we substitute their coordinates into the function $\mathbf F(x,y) = -2xy \, \mathbf{i} + x^2 \, \mathbf{j} \,\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(-2,1) & =-2(-2)(1)\,i+(-2)^{2}\,j=4\,i+4\,j \\ F(-1,-2) & =-2(-1)(-2)\,i+(-1)^{2}\,j=-4\,i+j \\ F(1,-1) & =-2(1)(-1)\,i+{1}^{2}\,j=2\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We now draw our vectors. At each point, we draw the vector associated with that point, placing the tail end of the vector on the point itself. This gives the following diagram.

Which of the following could be the function that generates the vector field above?

- $\mathbf F(x,y) = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$

- $\mathbf G(x,y) = 2 \, \mathbf{i}$

- $\mathbf H(x,y) = -x \, \mathbf{i}$
e-9441.worked_solution:
We notice the following:

- The vertical component (i.e., the $\mathbf j$ component) is zero for *every* vector in our vector field. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}
$$

- As we move away from the origin in the horizontal direction, our vectors' horizontal components (i.e., the $\mathbf i$ components) get longer. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
\mathbf G(x,y) = 2 \, \mathbf{i}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the diagram corresponds to the vector field $\mathbf{H}(x,y) = -x\, \mathbf{i}.$

- $\mathbf  F(x,y,z) = \mathbf j + \mathbf k$

- $\mathbf  G(x,y,z) = \mathbf k$

- $\mathbf  H(x,y,z) = z\,\mathbf k$

- $\mathbf  K(x,y,z) = -\mathbf k$
e-9473.worked_solution:
We notice the following:

- Each vector in our vector field is parallel to the $z$-axis. So, the $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ components of our vector field are zero everywhere. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \mathbf j + \mathbf k
$$

- Moreover, each vector in our vector field is pointing in the *negative* $z$-direction, so the $\mathbf k$ component of our vector field is negative. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
\mathbf G(x,y,z) = \mathbf k
$$

- Finally, we note that each vector in our vector field has the same length, so the $\mathbf i$ component of our vector field is constant. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
\mathbf H(x,y,z) = z\,\mathbf k
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the diagram corresponds to the vector field $\mathbf K(x,y,z) = -\mathbf k.$

$$
F(x,y)=i+j,\,K(x,y)=-i-2\,j
$$

G(x,y)=5\,j

after.worked_solution:
We notice the following:

- Each vector in our vector field is parallel to the $x$-axis. So, the $j$ and $k$ components of our vector field are zero everywhere. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
H(x,y,z)=i+j+k,\,
$$

- Moreover, each vector in our vector field is pointing in the *positive* $x$-direction, so the $i$ component of our vector field is positive. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
G(x,y,z)=-i
$$

- Finally, we note that each vector in our vector field has the same length, so the $i$ component of our vector field is constant. Therefore, we can rule out the following option:

$$
K(x,y,z)={e}^{x}\,i
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the diagram corresponds to the vector field $F(x,y,z)=i.$

$$

$$

$$
F(x,y,z)=j
$$

$$
G(x,y,z)=-{x}^{2}\,j
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the diagram doesn't correspond to any of the listed vector fields.
